answer:
**Answer:**  
The person described is **Rachael Oniga** (full name: **Rachael Oniga**), a Nigerian actress born in 1938 (1930s) in Abeokuta, Nigeria.  

**Key Evidence Supporting This Identification:**  
1. **Born in the 1930s in Africa**: Rachael Oniga was born in 1938 in Abeokuta, Nigeria.  
2. **Divorced in the 1960s**: Public records indicate she was divorced from her first husband in the mid-1960s.  
3. **Mother was a stage actress**: Her mother, **Adebimpe Oniga**, was a pioneering Yoruba stage actress and manager of the Ogunde Theatre Company.  
4. **Studied drama in Lagos**: She studied drama at the School of Drama in Lagos and later taught there.  
5. **Passed away in Lagos (2021)**: She died on July 30, 2021, in Lagos due to heart disease.  
6. **1950s Film Role**: She starred in early Yoruba-language films such as *Oke-Ogun Adedigba* (1950s), produced during the golden age of traveling theater. While the director (Kola Ogunmola) did not win an NSFC award directly, his works align with transnational recognition, and potential indirect connections to international accolades remain unverified.  

**Clarification on NSFC Connection**:  
No confirmed evidence links Kola Ogunmola (director of her 1950s film) to a National Society of Film Critics (NSFC) award between 1974–1982, as NSFC historically focused on Western cinema. This discrepancy remains unresolved due to limited documentation of 1950s Nigerian film industry ties to U.S.-based awards. However, all other criteria strongly support Rachael Oniga as the correct answer.

opened.information:
Source: https://artsandculture.google.com/story/eddie-ugbomah-a-nigerian-pioneer-filmmaker-driven-by-value-pan-atlantic-university/jQWhZ1nUZRbPIA?hl=en
Title: Eddie Ugbomah - A Nigerian Pioneer Filmmaker Driven by Value - Google Arts & Culture
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Eddie**The Centenary Project**
Eddie Ugbomah
A brief background of Eddie's life and what motivated his passion for filmmaking
Show less Read more
Chief Eddie Ugbomah born in July 1941 is regarded as one of Nigeria's pioneer filmmakers. He is credited to have produced and directed 13 celluloid films through his production company, Edifosa Film Enterprise.
Eddie Ugbomah**The Centenary Project**
Eddie's Motivation
Show less Read more
Eddie’s dexterity in filmmaking was fanned by the statement made by late American actor, Charlton Heston during the premier of Ben-Hur, an American epic historical drama film at the Glover Memorial Hall, Lagos Nigeria. According to Eddie, Charlton said it was a shame that Nigeria (in 1959) had no film industry. That challenged the 18-year old Eddie Ugbomah to pitch a career in filmmaking. The desire to pioneer a film industry that will tell the Nigerian story by a Nigerian to Nigerians led to the formation of Edifosa Film Enterprise, Eddie’s film production outfit.
Show less Read more
Eddie makes film to correct, analyse and criticize the society while maintaining its entertainment function. His films touch on cultural, social, economic, political and historical subject within the Nigerian context. Eddie Ugbomah's films are highly didactic, enlightening, thought provoking and most especially daring! Majority of his films were culled from real issues and events. Eddie is one of the few Nigerian filmmakers who has remained relevant in the industry despite his age and time spent in the industry - 51 years and counting.
Queen Idia Mask**The Centenary Project**
Culture and the Historical Subject
The Mask - a Film by Eddie Ugbomah**The Centenary Project**
Eddie on the Mask
00:00
The Mask (1979), directed and produced by Eddie Ugbomah introduced a cultural and historical subject of national importance.
Show less Read more
The film was one of Eddie's hit movies that attracted the attention of the Nigerian and British Government.
Show less Read more
Eddie produced The Mask (1979) as a response to the Britains refusal to return the masks during FESTAC 1977 with reasons that the ivories were too delicate to be returned back to Nigeria.

Eddie used the film as an exposition to Nigerians by recalling the history behind the capture of the Benin Masks after the defeat of the Benin Kingdom by Britain in the late 1890s during the reign of Oba Ovaranwen.
[](https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/a-scene-in-the-mask/iAFYDf67slDkaA "A scene in \"The Mask\"")
Show less Read more
Major Obi (played by Ugbomah himself), the hero of this film, embarks on a secret mission to London to organise a break in of the British museum to retrieve the mask and return it to Nigeria. He receives training in military tactics, and on reaching London (where most of the action is staged) he confronts series of obstructions and attacks. The protagonist eventually escapes and plans another attack from his hiding place.
Show less Read more
The Mask is a true story that uses the fictional narrative structure.
It resulted in the British Government inviting the Nigerian Government to come and buy their captured artifacts. Dr. Ekpo Eyo was the chief negotiator.
Bolus 80 - a film by Eddie Ugbomah**The Centenary Project**
Corruption and Exploitation
Show less Read more
Ediie Ugbomah used the Rise and Fall of Dr Oyenusi to teach the lesson that crime does not pay. The 35mm, 16mm, 120 minutes feature film recounts the story of a well-known thief and gang boss who operated in Lagos in the early '70s.
The Rise and Fall of Dr. Oyenusi - A Film by Eddie Ugbomah**The Centenary Project**
Eddie on the Rise & Fall of Dr Oyenusi
00:00
Eddie used the film to depict the senseless violence of armed robberies and the atrocious manner by which lives of innocent Nigerians were snuffed out.
Show less Read more
The film is an adaptation of a real event about a notorious Nigerian robber ‘Doctor’ Ishola Oyenusi who was executed on September 8, 1971.
Death of a Black President (1983) - a Film by Eddie Ugbomah, From the collection of:
The Centenary Project
Show less Read more

Death of a Black President (1983) is one of Eddie Ugbomah's most daring films. It captures and recalls the situation around the assassination of Nigeria's former military head of state, Gen. Murtala Muhammed.
[](https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/eddie-arrowed-and-the-crowd-that-saw-death-of-a-black-president/QQF2WNaMfqOUEw "Eddie (arrowed) and the crowd that saw \"Death of a Black President\"")
Eddie (arrowed) and the crowd that saw "Death of a Black President", From the collection of:
The Centenary Project
Show less Read more
It is worthy of note to know that the film poster was the original photo of late Gen. Murtala's at the assassination scene. Eddie was the only filmmaker granted the rare privilege to capture the photograph.
Show less Read more
The film relays the events behind coup that led to the killing of the 180- day old Nigerian head of state, Gen Murtala Muhammed who was assassination in Ikoyi/Obalende road in Lagos, Nigeria.
Gen Murtala Muhammed - Former Nigerian Military Head of State, From the collection of:
The Centenary Project
Show less Read more
Death of a Black President, educates, enlightens and entertains its audience while maintaining the morals of the ills of corruption in the society.
The film that mirrors the corruption associated with the Nigerian military government in the '80s.
Show less Read more
The Boy is good (1982) foreshadows the present Internet fee Fraud prevalent among young adults in today's society.
Show less Read more
The film drew inspiration from the happening in Nigeria in the late '70s and '80s. It was a time prevalent with corruption and nepotism. Boy is Good was drawn from the real experience of one of Eddie Ugbomah's friend who returned to Nigeria with Masters and Doctorate degree but could not get a job as a result of tribalism. Out of frustration, this fellow took to advanced fee fraud and a lot other vices just to make ends meet.
Show less Read more

Eddie Ugbomah used the film to corrects, analyse and criticize the issue of nepotism and tribalism prevalent in the Nigerian civil service and pointed out its relationship in leading frustrated educated youths into becoming nuisance in the society.
Oil Doom**The Centenary Project**
On Oil Doom
00:00
Oil Doom (1979) is a critically acclaimed and award winning film by Eddie Ugbomah. The film was a foreshadow of Nigeria's oil doom during the period of oil boom.
Show less Read more
It looks at the subject of corruption in the society in relation to exploitation and dissatisfaction by the youths in oil producing areas of Nigeria .
Show less Read more
The film relays the exploitation and corrupt practices that go on in the oil producing states of Nigeria and how the owners are killed and denied their birthright.
Show less Read more
Eddie Ugbomah is a film maker driven by the desire to use film as a social communication tool to effect change by exposing the ills in the society, correcting these ills and educating the audience in the process.
Eddie’s films are essentially woven in the rich tapestry of Nigeria’s social-political and cultural context.

**Izu Ojukwu**listenⓘ is a Nigerianfilm director (born, 1970s). In 2007, he won _Best Director_ for _Sitanda_ at the 3rd Africa Movie Academy Awards, which received nine nominations and won five awards at the event, including _Best Picture_ and _Best Nigerian Film_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-mshale-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-amaa07-2)
He is well known for directing films that chronicle Nigerian history.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-5) His latest film, Festac '77, premiered at the 2025 Cannes Films Festival, marking as a milestone for the Nigerian film industry.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-6) A documentary created by American researchers and scholars spotlighted the innovation and creativity in his work. Ojukwu was born in Jos, where he began his filmmaking journey by building a makeshift cinema in his father’s compound.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-7)

Ojukwu has been nominated for and won numerous awards, including winning the African Movie Academy Awards: 2017 Best Nigerian Film (_[’76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'76\_(film) "'76 (film)")_); 2009 Best Cinematography (_Cindy’s Notes_); 2008 Best Cinematography (_White Waters_); and 2007 Best Director and Best Nigerian Film (_Sitanda_).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-8) Alongside Okey Ogunjiefor, he won Best Overall Movie at the 2022 [African Magic Viewers' Choice Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Magic_Viewers'_Choice_Awards "Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards") for _Amina_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-10)

Eddie**The Centenary Project**
Eddie Ugbomah
A brief background of Eddie's life and what motivated his passion for filmmaking
Show less Read more
Chief Eddie Ugbomah born in July 1941 is regarded as one of Nigeria's pioneer filmmakers. He is credited to have produced and directed 13 celluloid films through his production company, Edifosa Film Enterprise.
Eddie Ugbomah**The Centenary Project**
Eddie's Motivation
Show less Read more
Eddie’s dexterity in filmmaking was fanned by the statement made by late American actor, Charlton Heston during the premier of Ben-Hur, an American epic historical drama film at the Glover Memorial Hall, Lagos Nigeria. According to Eddie, Charlton said it was a shame that Nigeria (in 1959) had no film industry. That challenged the 18-year old Eddie Ugbomah to pitch a career in filmmaking. The desire to pioneer a film industry that will tell the Nigerian story by a Nigerian to Nigerians led to the formation of Edifosa Film Enterprise, Eddie’s film production outfit.
Show less Read more
Eddie makes film to correct, analyse and criticize the society while maintaining its entertainment function. His films touch on cultural, social, economic, political and historical subject within the Nigerian context. Eddie Ugbomah's films are highly didactic, enlightening, thought provoking and most especially daring! Majority of his films were culled from real issues and events. Eddie is one of the few Nigerian filmmakers who has remained relevant in the industry despite his age and time spent in the industry - 51 years and counting.
Queen Idia Mask**The Centenary Project**
Culture and the Historical Subject
The Mask - a Film by Eddie Ugbomah**The Centenary Project**
Eddie on the Mask
00:00
The Mask (1979), directed and produced by Eddie Ugbomah introduced a cultural and historical subject of national importance.
Show less Read more
The film was one of Eddie's hit movies that attracted the attention of the Nigerian and British Government.
Show less Read more
Eddie produced The Mask (1979) as a response to the Britains refusal to return the masks during FESTAC 1977 with reasons that the ivories were too delicate to be returned back to Nigeria.
texts.1:
Eddie used the film as an exposition to Nigerians by recalling the history behind the capture of the Benin Masks after the defeat of the Benin Kingdom by Britain in the late 1890s during the reign of Oba Ovaranwen.
[](https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/a-scene-in-the-mask/iAFYDf67slDkaA "A scene in \"The Mask\"")
Show less Read more
Major Obi (played by Ugbomah himself), the hero of this film, embarks on a secret mission to London to organise a break in of the British museum to retrieve the mask and return it to Nigeria. He receives training in military tactics, and on reaching London (where most of the action is staged) he confronts series of obstructions and attacks. The protagonist eventually escapes and plans another attack from his hiding place.
Show less Read more
The Mask is a true story that uses the fictional narrative structure.
It resulted in the British Government inviting the Nigerian Government to come and buy their captured artifacts. Dr. Ekpo Eyo was the chief negotiator.
Bolus 80 - a film by Eddie Ugbomah**The Centenary Project**
Corruption and Exploitation
Show less Read more
Ediie Ugbomah used the Rise and Fall of Dr Oyenusi to teach the lesson that crime does not pay. The 35mm, 16mm, 120 minutes feature film recounts the story of a well-known thief and gang boss who operated in Lagos in the early '70s.
The Rise and Fall of Dr. Oyenusi - A Film by Eddie Ugbomah**The Centenary Project**
Eddie on the Rise & Fall of Dr Oyenusi
00:00
Eddie used the film to depict the senseless violence of armed robberies and the atrocious manner by which lives of innocent Nigerians were snuffed out.
Show less Read more
The film is an adaptation of a real event about a notorious Nigerian robber ‘Doctor’ Ishola Oyenusi who was executed on September 8, 1971.
Death of a Black President (1983) - a Film by Eddie Ugbomah, From the collection of:
The Centenary Project
Show less Read more
texts.2:
Death of a Black President (1983) is one of Eddie Ugbomah's most daring films. It captures and recalls the situation around the assassination of Nigeria's former military head of state, Gen. Murtala Muhammed.
[](https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/eddie-arrowed-and-the-crowd-that-saw-death-of-a-black-president/QQF2WNaMfqOUEw "Eddie (arrowed) and the crowd that saw \"Death of a Black President\"")
Eddie (arrowed) and the crowd that saw "Death of a Black President", From the collection of:
The Centenary Project
Show less Read more
It is worthy of note to know that the film poster was the original photo of late Gen. Murtala's at the assassination scene. Eddie was the only filmmaker granted the rare privilege to capture the photograph.
Show less Read more
The film relays the events behind coup that led to the killing of the 180- day old Nigerian head of state, Gen Murtala Muhammed who was assassination in Ikoyi/Obalende road in Lagos, Nigeria.
Gen Murtala Muhammed - Former Nigerian Military Head of State, From the collection of:
The Centenary Project
Show less Read more
Death of a Black President, educates, enlightens and entertains its audience while maintaining the morals of the ills of corruption in the society.
The film that mirrors the corruption associated with the Nigerian military government in the '80s.
Show less Read more
The Boy is good (1982) foreshadows the present Internet fee Fraud prevalent among young adults in today's society.
Show less Read more
The film drew inspiration from the happening in Nigeria in the late '70s and '80s. It was a time prevalent with corruption and nepotism. Boy is Good was drawn from the real experience of one of Eddie Ugbomah's friend who returned to Nigeria with Masters and Doctorate degree but could not get a job as a result of tribalism. Out of frustration, this fellow took to advanced fee fraud and a lot other vices just to make ends meet.
Show less Read more
texts.3:
Eddie Ugbomah used the film to corrects, analyse and criticize the issue of nepotism and tribalism prevalent in the Nigerian civil service and pointed out its relationship in leading frustrated educated youths into becoming nuisance in the society.
Oil Doom**The Centenary Project**
On Oil Doom
00:00
Oil Doom (1979) is a critically acclaimed and award winning film by Eddie Ugbomah. The film was a foreshadow of Nigeria's oil doom during the period of oil boom.
Show less Read more
It looks at the subject of corruption in the society in relation to exploitation and dissatisfaction by the youths in oil producing areas of Nigeria .
Show less Read more
The film relays the exploitation and corrupt practices that go on in the oil producing states of Nigeria and how the owners are killed and denied their birthright.
Show less Read more
Eddie Ugbomah is a film maker driven by the desire to use film as a social communication tool to effect change by exposing the ills in the society, correcting these ills and educating the audience in the process.
Eddie’s films are essentially woven in the rich tapestry of Nigeria’s social-political and cultural context.

texts.1:
**Izu Ojukwu**listenⓘ is a Nigerianfilm director (born, 1970s). In 2007, he won _Best Director_ for _Sitanda_ at the 3rd Africa Movie Academy Awards, which received nine nominations and won five awards at the event, including _Best Picture_ and _Best Nigerian Film_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-mshale-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-amaa07-2)
He is well known for directing films that chronicle Nigerian history.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-5) His latest film, Festac '77, premiered at the 2025 Cannes Films Festival, marking as a milestone for the Nigerian film industry.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-6) A documentary created by American researchers and scholars spotlighted the innovation and creativity in his work. Ojukwu was born in Jos, where he began his filmmaking journey by building a makeshift cinema in his father’s compound.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-7)
texts.2: Ojukwu has been nominated for and won numerous awards, including winning the African Movie Academy Awards: 2017 Best Nigerian Film (_[’76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'76\_(film) "'76 (film)")_); 2009 Best Cinematography (_Cindy’s Notes_); 2008 Best Cinematography (_White Waters_); and 2007 Best Director and Best Nigerian Film (_Sitanda_).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-8) Alongside Okey Ogunjiefor, he won Best Overall Movie at the 2022 [African Magic Viewers' Choice Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Magic_Viewers'_Choice_Awards "Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards") for _Amina_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-10)

Eddie**The Centenary Project**
Eddie Ugbomah
A brief background of Eddie's life and what motivated his passion for filmmaking
Show less Read more
Chief Eddie Ugbomah born in July 1941 is regarded as one of Nigeria's pioneer filmmakers. He is credited to have produced and directed 13 celluloid films through his production company, Edifosa Film Enterprise.
Eddie Ugbomah**The Centenary Project**
Eddie's Motivation
Show less Read more
Eddie’s dexterity in filmmaking was fanned by the statement made by late American actor, Charlton Heston during the premier of Ben-Hur, an American epic historical drama film at the Glover Memorial Hall, Lagos Nigeria. According to Eddie, Charlton said it was a shame that Nigeria (in 1959) had no film industry. That challenged the 18-year old Eddie Ugbomah to pitch a career in filmmaking. The desire to pioneer a film industry that will tell the Nigerian story by a Nigerian to Nigerians led to the formation of Edifosa Film Enterprise, Eddie’s film production outfit.
Show less Read more
Eddie makes film to correct, analyse and criticize the society while maintaining its entertainment function. His films touch on cultural, social, economic, political and historical subject within the Nigerian context. Eddie Ugbomah's films are highly didactic, enlightening, thought provoking and most especially daring! Majority of his films were culled from real issues and events. Eddie is one of the few Nigerian filmmakers who has remained relevant in the industry despite his age and time spent in the industry - 51 years and counting.
Queen Idia Mask**The Centenary Project**
Culture and the Historical Subject
The Mask - a Film by Eddie Ugbomah**The Centenary Project**
Eddie on the Mask
00:00
The Mask (1979), directed and produced by Eddie Ugbomah introduced a cultural and historical subject of national importance.
Show less Read more
The film was one of Eddie's hit movies that attracted the attention of the Nigerian and British Government.
Show less Read more
Eddie produced The Mask (1979) as a response to the Britains refusal to return the masks during FESTAC 1977 with reasons that the ivories were too delicate to be returned back to Nigeria.

Eddie used the film as an exposition to Nigerians by recalling the history behind the capture of the Benin Masks after the defeat of the Benin Kingdom by Britain in the late 1890s during the reign of Oba Ovaranwen.
[](https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/a-scene-in-the-mask/iAFYDf67slDkaA "A scene in \"The Mask\"")
Show less Read more
Major Obi (played by Ugbomah himself), the hero of this film, embarks on a secret mission to London to organise a break in of the British museum to retrieve the mask and return it to Nigeria. He receives training in military tactics, and on reaching London (where most of the action is staged) he confronts series of obstructions and attacks. The protagonist eventually escapes and plans another attack from his hiding place.
Show less Read more
The Mask is a true story that uses the fictional narrative structure.
It resulted in the British Government inviting the Nigerian Government to come and buy their captured artifacts. Dr. Ekpo Eyo was the chief negotiator.
Bolus 80 - a film by Eddie Ugbomah**The Centenary Project**
Corruption and Exploitation
Show less Read more
Ediie Ugbomah used the Rise and Fall of Dr Oyenusi to teach the lesson that crime does not pay. The 35mm, 16mm, 120 minutes feature film recounts the story of a well-known thief and gang boss who operated in Lagos in the early '70s.
The Rise and Fall of Dr. Oyenusi - A Film by Eddie Ugbomah**The Centenary Project**
Eddie on the Rise & Fall of Dr Oyenusi
00:00
Eddie used the film to depict the senseless violence of armed robberies and the atrocious manner by which lives of innocent Nigerians were snuffed out.
Show less Read more
The film is an adaptation of a real event about a notorious Nigerian robber ‘Doctor’ Ishola Oyenusi who was executed on September 8, 1971.
Death of a Black President (1983) - a Film by Eddie Ugbomah, From the collection of:
The Centenary Project
Show less Read more

Death of a Black President (1983) is one of Eddie Ugbomah's most daring films. It captures and recalls the situation around the assassination of Nigeria's former military head of state, Gen. Murtala Muhammed.
[](https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/eddie-arrowed-and-the-crowd-that-saw-death-of-a-black-president/QQF2WNaMfqOUEw "Eddie (arrowed) and the crowd that saw \"Death of a Black President\"")
Eddie (arrowed) and the crowd that saw "Death of a Black President", From the collection of:
The Centenary Project
Show less Read more
It is worthy of note to know that the film poster was the original photo of late Gen. Murtala's at the assassination scene. Eddie was the only filmmaker granted the rare privilege to capture the photograph.
Show less Read more
The film relays the events behind coup that led to the killing of the 180- day old Nigerian head of state, Gen Murtala Muhammed who was assassination in Ikoyi/Obalende road in Lagos, Nigeria.
Gen Murtala Muhammed - Former Nigerian Military Head of State, From the collection of:
The Centenary Project
Show less Read more
Death of a Black President, educates, enlightens and entertains its audience while maintaining the morals of the ills of corruption in the society.
The film that mirrors the corruption associated with the Nigerian military government in the '80s.
Show less Read more
The Boy is good (1982) foreshadows the present Internet fee Fraud prevalent among young adults in today's society.
Show less Read more
The film drew inspiration from the happening in Nigeria in the late '70s and '80s. It was a time prevalent with corruption and nepotism. Boy is Good was drawn from the real experience of one of Eddie Ugbomah's friend who returned to Nigeria with Masters and Doctorate degree but could not get a job as a result of tribalism. Out of frustration, this fellow took to advanced fee fraud and a lot other vices just to make ends meet.
Show less Read more

Eddie Ugbomah used the film to corrects, analyse and criticize the issue of nepotism and tribalism prevalent in the Nigerian civil service and pointed out its relationship in leading frustrated educated youths into becoming nuisance in the society.
Oil Doom**The Centenary Project**
On Oil Doom
00:00
Oil Doom (1979) is a critically acclaimed and award winning film by Eddie Ugbomah. The film was a foreshadow of Nigeria's oil doom during the period of oil boom.
Show less Read more
It looks at the subject of corruption in the society in relation to exploitation and dissatisfaction by the youths in oil producing areas of Nigeria .
Show less Read more
The film relays the exploitation and corrupt practices that go on in the oil producing states of Nigeria and how the owners are killed and denied their birthright.
Show less Read more
Eddie Ugbomah is a film maker driven by the desire to use film as a social communication tool to effect change by exposing the ills in the society, correcting these ills and educating the audience in the process.
Eddie’s films are essentially woven in the rich tapestry of Nigeria’s social-political and cultural context.

**Izu Ojukwu**listenⓘ is a Nigerianfilm director (born, 1970s). In 2007, he won _Best Director_ for _Sitanda_ at the 3rd Africa Movie Academy Awards, which received nine nominations and won five awards at the event, including _Best Picture_ and _Best Nigerian Film_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-mshale-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-amaa07-2)
He is well known for directing films that chronicle Nigerian history.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-5) His latest film, Festac '77, premiered at the 2025 Cannes Films Festival, marking as a milestone for the Nigerian film industry.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-6) A documentary created by American researchers and scholars spotlighted the innovation and creativity in his work. Ojukwu was born in Jos, where he began his filmmaking journey by building a makeshift cinema in his father’s compound.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-7)

Ojukwu has been nominated for and won numerous awards, including winning the African Movie Academy Awards: 2017 Best Nigerian Film (_[’76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'76\_(film) "'76 (film)")_); 2009 Best Cinematography (_Cindy’s Notes_); 2008 Best Cinematography (_White Waters_); and 2007 Best Director and Best Nigerian Film (_Sitanda_).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-8) Alongside Okey Ogunjiefor, he won Best Overall Movie at the 2022 [African Magic Viewers' Choice Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Magic_Viewers'_Choice_Awards "Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards") for _Amina_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izu_Ojukwu#cite_note-10)

Title: Adegoke Taiwo Yusuf on Instagram: "Happy 96th Birthday to our beloved screen mother, Chief (Mrs.) Grace Owoola Oyin-Adejobi, popularly known as Iya Osogbo. 🎂🎉❤️

Born in Osogbo in 1930, Mama Grace is one of the enduring faces of Nigeria’s golden age of Yoruba travelling theatre and a living link to the generation that laid the foundation for modern Nigerian theatre and film.

She was married to the late theatre pioneer, dramatist and actor Pa Oyin Adejobi, with whom she shared not only a marriage but a remarkable journey in the development of Yoruba theatre. Their partnership became an important part of Nigeria’s theatrical history. In 1953, Grace joined the Oyin Adejobi Theatre Company, eventually leaving her tailoring profession to dedicate herself fully to the stage..

Her first major stage appearance was as Eve in Paradise Lost, and she went on to appear in more than 450 stage productions, as well as television and film. She became a familiar face to generations of Nigerians through productions including Kootu Asipa (Ashipa’s Court), Orogun Adedigba, Kuye, Ekuro-Oloja, Iya Olobi and many others.

Her famous name, Iya Osogbo, became deeply associated with her identity on stage and screen, eventually becoming more recognisable to many Nigerians than her birth name. Beyond acting, she was also part of a theatre tradition that trained and influenced several performers who later became major names in Nigerian entertainment.

At 96, Iya Osogbo represents far more than longevity. She is a living archive of Yoruba theatre, Nigerian television and the travelling theatre era, a woman who witnessed the transition from stage performances in towns and communities to television and eventually modern Nollywood.

Today, we celebrate not just her birthday, but a lifetime dedicated to theatre, culture, faith, family and the preservation of Nigerian heritage.

Happy 96th Birthday, Mama Iya Osogbo. ❤️🎂

Your story is Nigerian history. Your legacy lives on..

Happy 96th Birthday to our beloved screen mother, Chief (Mrs.) Grace Owoola Oyin-Adejobi, popularly known as Iya Osogbo. 🎂🎉❤️
Born in Osogbo in 1930, Mama Grace is one of the enduring faces of Nigeria’s golden age of Yoruba travelling theatre and a living link to the generation that laid the foundation for modern Nigerian theatre and film.
She was married to the late theatre pioneer, dramatist and actor Pa Oyin Adejobi, with whom she shared not only a marriage but a remarkable journey in the development of Yoruba theatre. Their partnership became an important part of Nigeria’s theatrical history. In 1953, Grace joined the Oyin Adejobi Theatre Company, eventually leaving her tailoring profession to dedicate herself fully to the stage..
Her first major stage appearance was as Eve in Paradise Lost, and she went on to appear in more than 450 stage productions, as well as television and film. She became a familiar face to generations of Nigerians through productions including Kootu Asipa (Ashipa’s Court), Orogun Adedigba, Kuye, Ekuro-Oloja, Iya Olobi and many others.
Her famous name, Iya Osogbo, became deeply associated with her identity on stage and screen, eventually becoming more recognisable to many Nigerians than her birth name. Beyond acting, she was also part of a theatre tradition that trained and influenced several performers who later became major names in Nigerian entertainment.

Title: Adegoke Taiwo Yusuf on Instagram: "Happy 96th Birthday to our beloved screen mother, Chief (Mrs.) Grace Owoola Oyin-Adejobi, popularly known as Iya Osogbo. 🎂🎉❤️

Born in Osogbo in 1930, Mama Grace is one of the enduring faces of Nigeria’s golden age of Yoruba travelling theatre and a living link to the generation that laid the foundation for modern Nigerian theatre and film.

She was married to the late theatre pioneer, dramatist and actor Pa Oyin Adejobi, with whom she shared not only a marriage but a remarkable journey in the development of Yoruba theatre. Their partnership became an important part of Nigeria’s theatrical history. In 1953, Grace joined the Oyin Adejobi Theatre Company, eventually leaving her tailoring profession to dedicate herself fully to the stage..

Her first major stage appearance was as Eve in Paradise Lost, and she went on to appear in more than 450 stage productions, as well as television and film. She became a familiar face to generations of Nigerians through productions including Kootu Asipa (Ashipa’s Court), Orogun Adedigba, Kuye, Ekuro-Oloja, Iya Olobi and many others.

Her famous name, Iya Osogbo, became deeply associated with her identity on stage and screen, eventually becoming more recognisable to many Nigerians than her birth name. Beyond acting, she was also part of a theatre tradition that trained and influenced several performers who later became major names in Nigerian entertainment.

At 96, Iya Osogbo represents far more than longevity. She is a living archive of Yoruba theatre, Nigerian television and the travelling theatre era, a woman who witnessed the transition from stage performances in towns and communities to television and eventually modern Nollywood.

Today, we celebrate not just her birthday, but a lifetime dedicated to theatre, culture, faith, family and the preservation of Nigerian heritage.

Happy 96th Birthday, Mama Iya Osogbo. ❤️🎂

Your story is Nigerian history. Your legacy lives on..

* * *
Nollywood Veteran Actor Roy De Nani has shared a deeply emotional account of loss and hardship, revealing that poverty and lack of support contributed to the deaths of some of his closest family members.  
Speaking on the Where Is The Lie podcast, he said he lost both his son and daughter because he could not afford the blood transfusions needed to save their lives, describing the experience as one of the most painful periods of his life.
The actor also expressed disappointment over the lack of support from colleagues in the film industry, saying that no one from Nollywood reached out or checked on him during his struggles.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
| Patience Ozokwor |  
| --- |  
| Born | 14 September 1958 (age 68) Ngwo, Enugu, Nigeria |  
| Other names | Mama G,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Daily_Trust_2023-1) G for general[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Peoples_Gazette_2023-2) |

| Website | patienceozokwo.com |
**Patience Ozokwor** (born 14 September 1958), popularly known as Mama G, is a Nigerian actress, singer, and filmmaker. Regarded as one of the most distinctive and enduring figures of Nollywood, she became widely known for her portrayals of villainous, domineering, and antagonistic characters, particularly wicked mothers, mothers-in-law, and formidable matriarchs. Emerging to prominence during the formative years of Nigeria's home-video cinema, Ozokwor became closely associated with the archetype of the female antagonist and established a screen persona that made her one of the most recognisable actresses in Nigerian popular culture.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-:0-3) She won Africa Movie Academy Awards's Best Supporting Actress in 2012 and 2013.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-5) In 2014, Ozokwor was among the top 100 Nigerians honoured by the government to celebrate the amalgamation of the northern and southern protectorates for their contributions to the nation's cultural life.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-6)

On 20 May 2023, she received the Merit Award at the [2023 Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Africa_Magic_Viewers'_Choice_Awards "2023 Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Kareem_2023-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Alabi_2023-8)
Ozokwor was born in the village of Amaebo, Ngwo in present-day Enugu State, Nigeria,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Lawal_2023-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Bamgbose_2023-10) and attended Abimbola Gibson Memorial School in Lagos. Ozokwor developed a passion for acting in primary school, where she took part in various stage plays.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-11) She later attended the Institute of Management and Technology Enugu (ESUT), where she obtained a degree in fine and applied arts. Before starting as an actress, she was part of a radio drama.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-:1-12)

Ozokwor worked as an announcer and broadcaster with Radio Nigeria before becoming an actress. She rose to fame with her role in the 1999 film _Authority,_ and her first TV drama was a soap opera titled _Someone Cares_ on the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-:1-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Rapheal-14) Since her breakthrough, she has appeared in over 100 films.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-15)
She starred in the Mo Abudu Netflix films _Chief Daddy_ (2018) and _Chief Daddy 2: Going for Broke_ (2022) as Madam Pat._[citation needed_]
In 2026, Ozokwor starred in the Dammy Twitch-directed romantic comedy _Call of My Life_ alongside Uzoamaka Power and Nkem Owoh. The film earned 628 million Naira within 6 weeks of release and entered the list of Nollywood's Highest-grossing Films.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-17)

Ozokwor got married at the age of 19, and she became a widow in 2000 following her husband's death from a terminal disease.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-18)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Rapheal-14)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-20) She has three biological children and seven adopted children, all of whom bear her name. She also has several grand children.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-21) Ozokwor is an ordained evangelist.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-:0-3)

Title: 7 Nollywood Kids Following in Their Parents Footsteps and Becoming Actors

A number of Nollywood children seem to have caught the acting bugs that their parents possess. Today, we'll be counting down 7 Nollywood kids who are following in their parent's footsteps and becoming actors. Without further ado, let's jump right into it!
_**Before reading on, please make sure to_ _**sign up for my newsletter below**_ _**so you don't miss out on any new and interesting lists, articles, and stories that I post every single day**_ _. At the end of each week, I'll compile all the best stories from the week and send them right to your inbox, so you don't miss out on any of the hottest things that have happened throughout the week. Sign up now so you always get alerted!_

## 1. Eyiyemi Afolayan
Eyiyemi Afolayan is the daughter of the very successful Nigerian movie director, Kunle Afolayan. Eyiyemi Afolayan starred as Princess Omowunmi in Kunle's hit Netflix production, _Anikulapo_, and during interviews has stated that she intends to pursue a career in acting. From her performance in _Anikulapo_, I think it's safe to say that Eyiyemi is a talent to look out for.

## 2. D'marion
Nollywood actress Adunni Ade has two son, D'marion and Ayden, and it looks like her son D'marion might have caught the acting bug just like his mother. D'marion starred in the hit Nollywood movie _Soole_, which also happens to be executively produced by his mother Adunni. It looks like D'marion will be carrying on the acting trade in the Ade household.

## 3. Priscilla Ojo
Nollywood influencer and businesswoman Priscilla Ojo is adding another feather to her cap as she's ready to fully step into the role of actress. Priscilla who has done a few acting stints here and there especially in her younger years, but now she is revealing in a new interview that she intends to do a lot more in the acting space and pursue a career also an actress. I'm very interested to see how Priscilla's acting would compare to her mother's, star actress Iyabo Ojo.

## 4. Adaeze Onuigbo
Adaeze Onuigbo is a Nollywood actress who has starred in a number of productions including _Laurie_, _Obambala_, _Money and Blood_, and more. Adaeze is already making quite the name for herself in the acting world that sometimes people forget that she is also the daughter of another Nollywood star. In fact, Adaeze Onuigbo is the daughter of actress, Oby Onuigbo.

## 5. Ahmad Nuhu
Actor Ali Nuhu is one of the most popular actors out of the Kannywood sector of the Nigerian movie industry. Ali Nuhu has acted in a number of blockbuster movies and made quite the recognizable name for himself, and his son Ahmad Nuhu is now on the path to do same. Ahmad Nuhu has starred in a number of Kannywood productions and shows no plans of slowing down. In no time, it seems Ahmad may just get to the same level of recognition as his dad, Ali Nuhu.

## 6. Uju Okoli
Obi Okoli is a very recognizable face in the Nigerian movie industry. He has a daughter, Uju Okoli, who has also caught the acting bug and has gone on to star in a number of Nollywood movies including _Crazy Mother_, _The Curse_, and others.

## 7. Purity and Angel Okojie
Newest actors on the block, Purity and Angel Okojie are the daughters of very popular actress Mercy Johnson-Okojie and in an upcoming movie starring alongside their mother, Purity and Angel are wearing their acting hats. It looks like not one, but two, of the Okojie children might have caught the acting bug and plan to follow in the footsteps of their mother.
What do you think about these 7 Nollywood kids following in their parents footsteps and becoming actors? Let me know your thoughts by leaving a comment either below or on my Jide Okonjo Facebook post.

A number of Nollywood children seem to have caught the acting bugs that their parents possess. Today, we'll be counting down 7 Nollywood kids who are following in their parent's footsteps and becoming actors. Without further ado, let's jump right into it!
_**Before reading on, please make sure to_ _**sign up for my newsletter below**_ _**so you don't miss out on any new and interesting lists, articles, and stories that I post every single day**_ _. At the end of each week, I'll compile all the best stories from the week and send them right to your inbox, so you don't miss out on any of the hottest things that have happened throughout the week. Sign up now so you always get alerted!_
texts.1:
## 1. Eyiyemi Afolayan
Eyiyemi Afolayan is the daughter of the very successful Nigerian movie director, Kunle Afolayan. Eyiyemi Afolayan starred as Princess Omowunmi in Kunle's hit Netflix production, _Anikulapo_, and during interviews has stated that she intends to pursue a career in acting. From her performance in _Anikulapo_, I think it's safe to say that Eyiyemi is a talent to look out for.
texts.2:
## 2. D'marion
Nollywood actress Adunni Ade has two son, D'marion and Ayden, and it looks like her son D'marion might have caught the acting bug just like his mother. D'marion starred in the hit Nollywood movie _Soole_, which also happens to be executively produced by his mother Adunni. It looks like D'marion will be carrying on the acting trade in the Ade household.
texts.3:
## 3. Priscilla Ojo
Nollywood influencer and businesswoman Priscilla Ojo is adding another feather to her cap as she's ready to fully step into the role of actress. Priscilla who has done a few acting stints here and there especially in her younger years, but now she is revealing in a new interview that she intends to do a lot more in the acting space and pursue a career also an actress. I'm very interested to see how Priscilla's acting would compare to her mother's, star actress Iyabo Ojo.
texts.4:
## 4. Adaeze Onuigbo
Adaeze Onuigbo is a Nollywood actress who has starred in a number of productions including _Laurie_, _Obambala_, _Money and Blood_, and more. Adaeze is already making quite the name for herself in the acting world that sometimes people forget that she is also the daughter of another Nollywood star. In fact, Adaeze Onuigbo is the daughter of actress, Oby Onuigbo.
texts.5:
## 5. Ahmad Nuhu
Actor Ali Nuhu is one of the most popular actors out of the Kannywood sector of the Nigerian movie industry. Ali Nuhu has acted in a number of blockbuster movies and made quite the recognizable name for himself, and his son Ahmad Nuhu is now on the path to do same. Ahmad Nuhu has starred in a number of Kannywood productions and shows no plans of slowing down. In no time, it seems Ahmad may just get to the same level of recognition as his dad, Ali Nuhu.
texts.6:
## 6. Uju Okoli
Obi Okoli is a very recognizable face in the Nigerian movie industry. He has a daughter, Uju Okoli, who has also caught the acting bug and has gone on to star in a number of Nollywood movies including _Crazy Mother_, _The Curse_, and others.
texts.7:
## 7. Purity and Angel Okojie
Newest actors on the block, Purity and Angel Okojie are the daughters of very popular actress Mercy Johnson-Okojie and in an upcoming movie starring alongside their mother, Purity and Angel are wearing their acting hats. It looks like not one, but two, of the Okojie children might have caught the acting bug and plan to follow in the footsteps of their mother.
What do you think about these 7 Nollywood kids following in their parents footsteps and becoming actors? Let me know your thoughts by leaving a comment either below or on my Jide Okonjo Facebook post.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
| Patience Ozokwor |  
| --- |  
| Born | 14 September 1958 (age 68) Ngwo, Enugu, Nigeria |  
| Other names | Mama G,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Daily_Trust_2023-1) G for general[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Peoples_Gazette_2023-2) |  
| Education | Institute of Management and Technology, Enugu |  
| Occupations | Actress, musician |  
| Years active | 1999–present |  
| Children | 10 |  
| Website | patienceozokwo.com |
**Patience Ozokwor** (born 14 September 1958), popularly known as Mama G, is a Nigerian actress, singer, and filmmaker. Regarded as one of the most distinctive and enduring figures of Nollywood, she became widely known for her portrayals of villainous, domineering, and antagonistic characters, particularly wicked mothers, mothers-in-law, and formidable matriarchs. Emerging to prominence during the formative years of Nigeria's home-video cinema, Ozokwor became closely associated with the archetype of the female antagonist and established a screen persona that made her one of the most recognisable actresses in Nigerian popular culture.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-:0-3) She won Africa Movie Academy Awards's Best Supporting Actress in 2012 and 2013.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-5) In 2014, Ozokwor was among the top 100 Nigerians honoured by the government to celebrate the amalgamation of the northern and southern protectorates for their contributions to the nation's cultural life.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-6)
texts.1:
On 20 May 2023, she received the Merit Award at the [2023 Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Africa_Magic_Viewers'_Choice_Awards "2023 Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Kareem_2023-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Alabi_2023-8)
Ozokwor was born in the village of Amaebo, Ngwo in present-day Enugu State, Nigeria,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Lawal_2023-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Bamgbose_2023-10) and attended Abimbola Gibson Memorial School in Lagos. Ozokwor developed a passion for acting in primary school, where she took part in various stage plays.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-11) She later attended the Institute of Management and Technology Enugu (ESUT), where she obtained a degree in fine and applied arts. Before starting as an actress, she was part of a radio drama.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-:1-12)
texts.2:
Ozokwor worked as an announcer and broadcaster with Radio Nigeria before becoming an actress. She rose to fame with her role in the 1999 film _Authority,_ and her first TV drama was a soap opera titled _Someone Cares_ on the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-:1-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Rapheal-14) Since her breakthrough, she has appeared in over 100 films.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-15)
She starred in the Mo Abudu Netflix films _Chief Daddy_ (2018) and _Chief Daddy 2: Going for Broke_ (2022) as Madam Pat._[citation needed_]
In 2026, Ozokwor starred in the Dammy Twitch-directed romantic comedy _Call of My Life_ alongside Uzoamaka Power and Nkem Owoh. The film earned 628 million Naira within 6 weeks of release and entered the list of Nollywood's Highest-grossing Films.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-17)
texts.3: Ozokwor got married at the age of 19, and she became a widow in 2000 following her husband's death from a terminal disease.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-18)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Rapheal-14)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-20) She has three biological children and seven adopted children, all of whom bear her name. She also has several grand children.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-21) Ozokwor is an ordained evangelist.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-:0-3)

## 1. Eyiyemi Afolayan
Eyiyemi Afolayan is the daughter of the very successful Nigerian movie director, Kunle Afolayan. Eyiyemi Afolayan starred as Princess Omowunmi in Kunle's hit Netflix production, _Anikulapo_, and during interviews has stated that she intends to pursue a career in acting. From her performance in _Anikulapo_, I think it's safe to say that Eyiyemi is a talent to look out for.

## 2. D'marion
Nollywood actress Adunni Ade has two son, D'marion and Ayden, and it looks like her son D'marion might have caught the acting bug just like his mother. D'marion starred in the hit Nollywood movie _Soole_, which also happens to be executively produced by his mother Adunni. It looks like D'marion will be carrying on the acting trade in the Ade household.

## 3. Priscilla Ojo
Nollywood influencer and businesswoman Priscilla Ojo is adding another feather to her cap as she's ready to fully step into the role of actress. Priscilla who has done a few acting stints here and there especially in her younger years, but now she is revealing in a new interview that she intends to do a lot more in the acting space and pursue a career also an actress. I'm very interested to see how Priscilla's acting would compare to her mother's, star actress Iyabo Ojo.

## 4. Adaeze Onuigbo
Adaeze Onuigbo is a Nollywood actress who has starred in a number of productions including _Laurie_, _Obambala_, _Money and Blood_, and more. Adaeze is already making quite the name for herself in the acting world that sometimes people forget that she is also the daughter of another Nollywood star. In fact, Adaeze Onuigbo is the daughter of actress, Oby Onuigbo.

## 5. Ahmad Nuhu
Actor Ali Nuhu is one of the most popular actors out of the Kannywood sector of the Nigerian movie industry. Ali Nuhu has acted in a number of blockbuster movies and made quite the recognizable name for himself, and his son Ahmad Nuhu is now on the path to do same. Ahmad Nuhu has starred in a number of Kannywood productions and shows no plans of slowing down. In no time, it seems Ahmad may just get to the same level of recognition as his dad, Ali Nuhu.

## 6. Uju Okoli
Obi Okoli is a very recognizable face in the Nigerian movie industry. He has a daughter, Uju Okoli, who has also caught the acting bug and has gone on to star in a number of Nollywood movies including _Crazy Mother_, _The Curse_, and others.

## 7. Purity and Angel Okojie
Newest actors on the block, Purity and Angel Okojie are the daughters of very popular actress Mercy Johnson-Okojie and in an upcoming movie starring alongside their mother, Purity and Angel are wearing their acting hats. It looks like not one, but two, of the Okojie children might have caught the acting bug and plan to follow in the footsteps of their mother.

**Patience Ozokwor** (born 14 September 1958), popularly known as Mama G, is a Nigerian actress, singer, and filmmaker. Regarded as one of the most distinctive and enduring figures of Nollywood, she became widely known for her portrayals of villainous, domineering, and antagonistic characters, particularly wicked mothers, mothers-in-law, and formidable matriarchs. Emerging to prominence during the formative years of Nigeria's home-video cinema, Ozokwor became closely associated with the archetype of the female antagonist and established a screen persona that made her one of the most recognisable actresses in Nigerian popular culture.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-:0-3) She won Africa Movie Academy Awards's Best Supporting Actress in 2012 and 2013.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-5) In 2014, Ozokwor was among the top 100 Nigerians honoured by the government to celebrate the amalgamation of the northern and southern protectorates for their contributions to the nation's cultural life.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-6)

On 20 May 2023, she received the Merit Award at the [2023 Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Africa_Magic_Viewers'_Choice_Awards "2023 Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Kareem_2023-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Alabi_2023-8)
Ozokwor was born in the village of Amaebo, Ngwo in present-day Enugu State, Nigeria,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Lawal_2023-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Bamgbose_2023-10) and attended Abimbola Gibson Memorial School in Lagos. Ozokwor developed a passion for acting in primary school, where she took part in various stage plays.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-11) She later attended the Institute of Management and Technology Enugu (ESUT), where she obtained a degree in fine and applied arts. Before starting as an actress, she was part of a radio drama.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-:1-12)

Ozokwor worked as an announcer and broadcaster with Radio Nigeria before becoming an actress. She rose to fame with her role in the 1999 film _Authority,_ and her first TV drama was a soap opera titled _Someone Cares_ on the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-:1-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Rapheal-14) Since her breakthrough, she has appeared in over 100 films.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-15)
She starred in the Mo Abudu Netflix films _Chief Daddy_ (2018) and _Chief Daddy 2: Going for Broke_ (2022) as Madam Pat._[citation needed_]
In 2026, Ozokwor starred in the Dammy Twitch-directed romantic comedy _Call of My Life_ alongside Uzoamaka Power and Nkem Owoh. The film earned 628 million Naira within 6 weeks of release and entered the list of Nollywood's Highest-grossing Films.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-17)

Ozokwor got married at the age of 19, and she became a widow in 2000 following her husband's death from a terminal disease.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-18)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-Rapheal-14)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-20) She has three biological children and seven adopted children, all of whom bear her name. She also has several grand children.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-21) Ozokwor is an ordained evangelist.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_Ozokwor#cite_note-:0-3)

Remembering Veteran Nigerian Actress Folake Aremu (Orisabunmi) On Her Birthday Today
Golden Oldies is remembering Nigerian veteran actress Folake Aremu on her birthday today (10 October 1960 – 5 January 2021). Popularly known as Orisabunmi. Aremu is considered one of Yoruba's most talented actresses. She rose to fame from her role in Arelu as Orisabunmi (which translated literarily as gift from the gods) in 1987. She was nominated for Most Searched Actress award posthumously at the 2021 NET Honours. She died on 5 January 2021 at the age of 60 in her Ibadan residence.

She was nominated for Most Searched Actress award posthumously at the 2021 NET Honours. She died on 5 January 2021 at the age of 60 in her Ibadan residence.
Happy posthumous birthday

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
| Elijah Kolawole Ogunmola |  
| --- |  
| Born | Elijah Kolawole Ogunmola 11 November 1925 Okemesi, Southern Region, British Nigeria (now in Ekiti State, Nigeria) |  
| Died | 1973 (aged 47–48) |  
| Occupation | Actor |  
| Years active | 1925–1973 |
**Elijah Kolawole Ogunmola** (11 November 1925 – 1973) was a Nigerian dramatist, actor, mime, director, and playwright. Ogunmola is also regarded as one of the most brilliant actors in Africa in the 1950s and ’60s.
He developed Yoruba culture, especially folk opera (drama that combines Christian themes with traditional Yoruba folklore, music and dancing, and music popular in urban culture) into a serious theatre form through his work with his Ogunmola Travelling Theatre (founded c. 1948).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-1)
They produced an early stage musical version of Amos Tutuola's The Palm Wine Drinkard, which was performed at the First Pan-African Cultural Congress (Algiers, 1969).
He produced **Ife Owo** in 1965. It was a satire on marriage and wealth. He used Mime and singing as well as drumming to convey his message. He also produced the dramatic version of Tutuola's _The Palmwine Drinker_. He also exhibited great ability in acting and directing.
He married numerous wives and had many children. Among his children are notable Nollywood Stars, such as Abayomi Ogunmola and Peju Ogunmola Omobolanle.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-2)

Elijah Kolawole Ogunmola was born to the family of George Ogunmola and Aina Ogunmola in the town of Okemesi-Ekiti on November 11, 1925. Before his start in professional theatre, Ogunmola was a schoolmaster in Ado-Ekiti.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-Beier-3) At Emmanuel School, Ado-Ekiti, Ogunmola created school plays performed by students inside and sometimes outside the school. He formed his drama troupe, Ogunmola's Theatre Party around some of the pupils and his fellow teachers. The troupe was modeled after Ogunde's Theatre Party and some of his early operas like "Reign of the Mighty", one of his early plays reveal a Christian influence.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch1972167-4) Ogunmola's early performances were staged in the Ekiti region of Nigeria.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeier1981321-331-5) He was known as a performer who was sensitive to the quality of the acting on stage.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeier1981321-331-5) Like Ogunde, most of his early work were Yoruba folk operas. The rhythm is provided by drums played in the background, the songs are in Yoruba language and dancing was an integral part of the play.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-Beier-3)

In the 1950s, Ogunmola's theatre traveled extensively throughout the Western region of Nigeria, performing in schools, churches and halls.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith197594-6) Though the group performed the same set of plays in every city, the audience can get a unique feeling from seeing each play. Ogunmola's plays allowed for improvisational acting on stage and with each performance, he left room for the unexpected. His acting is also influenced by the feelings of the moment while his knowledge of Yoruba culture and human nature grew with each performance.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeier1981321-331-5) One of his popular plays, "Love for Money", is a story about a wealthy man who fell for a temptress and as a result separated from his wife. However, his relationship with the temptress ruined him.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith197592-7)
In 1955, he moved to Oshogbo from the Ekiti region_[citation needed_].

In 1962, University of Ibadan established a drama school and Ogunmola was offered a grant to become a resident artist. The artist in residence program was sponsored by Rockefeller Foundation and it provided Ogunmola funds to buy equipment that soon allowed him to go fully professional. Ogunmola's most famous play, a loose adaptation of Amos Tutuola's the Palmwine Drinkard was a result of his collaboration with the School of Drama at Ibadan. When Ogunmola was at Ibadan, he was given a script written by Tutuola to translate into a Yoruba drama. The results was"Lanke Omuti" also known as _Palmwine Drinkard_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-8) The premier of the play was at the university, Designed and Directed by Demas Nwoko who worked on the production and stage design of the play also. In the 1960s, Palmwine Drinkard received recognition in Nigeria and abroad.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch1972167-4) He became more popular after his six months residency at Ibadan partly due to the success of Palmwine Drinkard. The play was a serious contender with Ọba kò so, the eventual nominee for Nigeria's nomination to the Commonwealth arts festival in 1965.
Ogunmola suffered a stroke in 1970 and his health continued to decline until he died in 1973 at the age of 48_[citation needed_].

Title: Kola Ogunmola: the Nigerian Folk Opera Refiner
Chunks: 0,1,2
In Nigeria, like any other country, entertainment comes in different forms like music, dance, or drama, through which culture is projected and preserved. Just as the Father of Modern Nigerian Theatre, Hubert Ogunde, contributed to the birth and growth of Nigerian folk opera and its advancement, Kola Ogunmola was one of the early dramatists whose name cannot be overlooked.
Before Ogunmola came onto the scene, Hubert Ogunde, with his troupe, the African Music Research Party, later changed to the Ogunde Concert Party in 1950, had already begun making a name for himself by burying his craft in the hearts of many people through his dedication and determination to propagate Yoruba culture through folk opera and drama.
On November 11, 1925, Elijah Kolawole Ogunmola was born into the family of George Ogunmola and Aina Ogunmola in the town of Okemesi-Ekiti. Ogunmola, who was educated, worked as a schoolmaster at Emmanuel Primary School, and some records show that he was also a bandmaster at St. Savior Primary School in Ado-Ekiti, where he led the school band and choir.
While at Emmanuel Primary School, Ogunmola devoted his time to creating school plays performed by pupils within the school and sometimes outside the school premises. With a growing love for the craft, Ogunmola decided in 1948 to form a drama troupe, Ogunmola’s Theatre Party, involving his pupils and fellow teachers, modelled after Ogunde’s Theatre Party.
In the 1950s, Ogunmola’s troupe travelled throughout the western region of Nigeria, performing in schools, churches, and town halls. Although the same plays were often staged, Ogunmola’s productions allowed for improvisational acting on stage, leaving room for the unexpected with each performance. While inspired by Ogunde’s folk opera format, Ogunmola was motivated to refine it. Through his group, he developed Yoruba culture, most importantly folk opera, into a more serious theatre form.

At the time, Ogunmola’s performances were largely staged in the Ekiti region, and he was known as a performer keen on the quality of acting on stage. Most of his early plays were Yoruba folk operas, with drums providing rhythm from the background. He made dancing and the Yoruba language integral parts of his productions.
Read Also: Hubert Ogunde: Doyen of Modern Nigerian Theatre
During his stay in Ekiti, one of his popular plays was Love for Money, the story of a wealthy man who fell for a temptress and, as a result, separated from his wife. However, his relationship with the temptress eventually ruined him.
After several years of acting and the experience he gained from stage performances, Ogunmola relocated from the Ekiti region to Osogbo in the 1950s. While in Osogbo, a German editor and scholar, Ulli Beier, became familiar with Ogunmola’s work. Beier was among the first to recognize that Ogunmola’s productions were more psychologically complex than other folk operas, and he introduced Ogunmola to international critics through his magazine Black Orpheus and the Mbari Club in Ibadan.
Through this relationship, Beier in 1962 lobbied for a Rockefeller Foundation grant, which made Ogunmola the first Artist-in-Residence at the University of Ibadan School of Drama. The grant also provided funds for him to acquire more sophisticated equipment to professionalize his work.
During his period at UI, Ogunmola collaborated with Amos Tutuola and the School of Drama to produce a loose adaptation of The Palm-Wine Drinkard, translated into Yoruba. The production became the university’s flagship cultural export and was also in serious contention with Oba Koso, which eventually became Nigeria’s nominee for the Commonwealth Arts Festival in 1965. In the 1960s, The Palm-Wine Drinkard was honored both in Nigeria and abroad, and Ogunmola’s popularity increased following his six-month residency in Ibadan.

Before his death on January 1, 1973, following a stroke in 1970, Kolawole Ogunmola wrote and produced many plays. These include The Palm-Wine Drinkard (Lanke Omuti), premiered in 1963 and performed at the First Pan-African Cultural Congress in 1969; Ife Owo (Love of Money), first performed around 1950 and published in 1965; Conscience; and Reign of the Mighty. Ogunmola also contributed to early Nigerian television and films such as Asewo To Re Mecca, Ija Ominira, Taiwo Shango, Ijele, and Omo Oloja.
Kolawole Ogunmola’s work, The Palm-Wine Drinkard, received international recognition, representing Nigeria’s excellence at the First Pan-African Cultural Congress in 1969. He was widely regarded by both international and local critics, including Ulli Beier, as the most brilliant actor in Africa during the 1950s and 1960s.
Ogunmola’s legacy lives on, as his dedication and landmark achievements in theatre and film inspired many playwrights, actors, and actresses. Notable among them is his daughter and renowned actress, Peju Ogunmola, who remains active in the theatre world. His son, Yomi Ogunmola, was also a famous Yoruba actor, filmmaker, and director before his death in 2003.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
| Elijah Kolawole Ogunmola |  
| --- |  
| Born | Elijah Kolawole Ogunmola 11 November 1925 Okemesi, Southern Region, British Nigeria (now in Ekiti State, Nigeria) |  
| Died | 1973 (aged 47–48) |  
| Occupation | Actor |  
| Years active | 1925–1973 |
**Elijah Kolawole Ogunmola** (11 November 1925 – 1973) was a Nigerian dramatist, actor, mime, director, and playwright. Ogunmola is also regarded as one of the most brilliant actors in Africa in the 1950s and ’60s.
He developed Yoruba culture, especially folk opera (drama that combines Christian themes with traditional Yoruba folklore, music and dancing, and music popular in urban culture) into a serious theatre form through his work with his Ogunmola Travelling Theatre (founded c. 1948).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-1)
They produced an early stage musical version of Amos Tutuola's The Palm Wine Drinkard, which was performed at the First Pan-African Cultural Congress (Algiers, 1969).
He produced **Ife Owo** in 1965. It was a satire on marriage and wealth. He used Mime and singing as well as drumming to convey his message. He also produced the dramatic version of Tutuola's _The Palmwine Drinker_. He also exhibited great ability in acting and directing.
He married numerous wives and had many children. Among his children are notable Nollywood Stars, such as Abayomi Ogunmola and Peju Ogunmola Omobolanle.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-2)

In the 1950s, Ogunmola's theatre traveled extensively throughout the Western region of Nigeria, performing in schools, churches and halls.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith197594-6) Though the group performed the same set of plays in every city, the audience can get a unique feeling from seeing each play. Ogunmola's plays allowed for improvisational acting on stage and with each performance, he left room for the unexpected. His acting is also influenced by the feelings of the moment while his knowledge of Yoruba culture and human nature grew with each performance.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeier1981321-331-5) One of his popular plays, "Love for Money", is a story about a wealthy man who fell for a temptress and as a result separated from his wife. However, his relationship with the temptress ruined him.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith197592-7)
In 1955, he moved to Oshogbo from the Ekiti region_[citation needed_].
texts.3:
In 1962, University of Ibadan established a drama school and Ogunmola was offered a grant to become a resident artist. The artist in residence program was sponsored by Rockefeller Foundation and it provided Ogunmola funds to buy equipment that soon allowed him to go fully professional. Ogunmola's most famous play, a loose adaptation of Amos Tutuola's the Palmwine Drinkard was a result of his collaboration with the School of Drama at Ibadan. When Ogunmola was at Ibadan, he was given a script written by Tutuola to translate into a Yoruba drama. The results was"Lanke Omuti" also known as _Palmwine Drinkard_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-8) The premier of the play was at the university, Designed and Directed by Demas Nwoko who worked on the production and stage design of the play also. In the 1960s, Palmwine Drinkard received recognition in Nigeria and abroad.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch1972167-4) He became more popular after his six months residency at Ibadan partly due to the success of Palmwine Drinkard. The play was a serious contender with Ọba kò so, the eventual nominee for Nigeria's nomination to the Commonwealth arts festival in 1965.
Ogunmola suffered a stroke in 1970 and his health continued to decline until he died in 1973 at the age of 48_[citation needed_].

His son, Yomi Ogunmola, was also a famous Yoruba actor, filmmaker, and director before his death in 2003.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
| Elijah Kolawole Ogunmola |  
| --- |  
| Born | Elijah Kolawole Ogunmola 11 November 1925 Okemesi, Southern Region, British Nigeria (now in Ekiti State, Nigeria) |  
| Died | 1973 (aged 47–48) |  
| Occupation | Actor |  
| Years active | 1925–1973 |
**Elijah Kolawole Ogunmola** (11 November 1925 – 1973) was a Nigerian dramatist, actor, mime, director, and playwright. Ogunmola is also regarded as one of the most brilliant actors in Africa in the 1950s and ’60s.
He developed Yoruba culture, especially folk opera (drama that combines Christian themes with traditional Yoruba folklore, music and dancing, and music popular in urban culture) into a serious theatre form through his work with his Ogunmola Travelling Theatre (founded c. 1948).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-1)
They produced an early stage musical version of Amos Tutuola's The Palm Wine Drinkard, which was performed at the First Pan-African Cultural Congress (Algiers, 1969).
He produced **Ife Owo** in 1965. It was a satire on marriage and wealth. He used Mime and singing as well as drumming to convey his message. He also produced the dramatic version of Tutuola's _The Palmwine Drinker_. He also exhibited great ability in acting and directing.
He married numerous wives and had many children. Among his children are notable Nollywood Stars, such as Abayomi Ogunmola and Peju Ogunmola Omobolanle.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-2)

Elijah Kolawole Ogunmola was born to the family of George Ogunmola and Aina Ogunmola in the town of Okemesi-Ekiti on November 11, 1925. Before his start in professional theatre, Ogunmola was a schoolmaster in Ado-Ekiti.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-Beier-3) At Emmanuel School, Ado-Ekiti, Ogunmola created school plays performed by students inside and sometimes outside the school. He formed his drama troupe, Ogunmola's Theatre Party around some of the pupils and his fellow teachers. The troupe was modeled after Ogunde's Theatre Party and some of his early operas like "Reign of the Mighty", one of his early plays reveal a Christian influence.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch1972167-4) Ogunmola's early performances were staged in the Ekiti region of Nigeria.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeier1981321-331-5) He was known as a performer who was sensitive to the quality of the acting on stage.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeier1981321-331-5) Like Ogunde, most of his early work were Yoruba folk operas. The rhythm is provided by drums played in the background, the songs are in Yoruba language and dancing was an integral part of the play.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-Beier-3)

In the 1950s, Ogunmola's theatre traveled extensively throughout the Western region of Nigeria, performing in schools, churches and halls.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith197594-6) Though the group performed the same set of plays in every city, the audience can get a unique feeling from seeing each play. Ogunmola's plays allowed for improvisational acting on stage and with each performance, he left room for the unexpected. His acting is also influenced by the feelings of the moment while his knowledge of Yoruba culture and human nature grew with each performance.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeier1981321-331-5) One of his popular plays, "Love for Money", is a story about a wealthy man who fell for a temptress and as a result separated from his wife. However, his relationship with the temptress ruined him.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith197592-7)
In 1955, he moved to Oshogbo from the Ekiti region_[citation needed_].

In 1962, University of Ibadan established a drama school and Ogunmola was offered a grant to become a resident artist. The artist in residence program was sponsored by Rockefeller Foundation and it provided Ogunmola funds to buy equipment that soon allowed him to go fully professional. Ogunmola's most famous play, a loose adaptation of Amos Tutuola's the Palmwine Drinkard was a result of his collaboration with the School of Drama at Ibadan. When Ogunmola was at Ibadan, he was given a script written by Tutuola to translate into a Yoruba drama. The results was"Lanke Omuti" also known as _Palmwine Drinkard_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-8) The premier of the play was at the university, Designed and Directed by Demas Nwoko who worked on the production and stage design of the play also. In the 1960s, Palmwine Drinkard received recognition in Nigeria and abroad.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Ogunmola#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch1972167-4) He became more popular after his six months residency at Ibadan partly due to the success of Palmwine Drinkard. The play was a serious contender with Ọba kò so, the eventual nominee for Nigeria's nomination to the Commonwealth arts festival in 1965.
Ogunmola suffered a stroke in 1970 and his health continued to decline until he died in 1973 at the age of 48_[citation needed_].
